demographics.narrative:
The 2025 census counted 122,972,528 residents on 1 October 2025, down 3.17 million, or 2.5 percent, from 2020.{{1}} Japanese nationals numbered about 119.13 million, down 3.5 percent, while foreign residents reached 3.84 million (3.1 percent of the total), up 39.8 percent.{{1}} People aged 65 and over numbered 36.14 million (29.4 percent) and children under 15 numbered 13.35 million (10.9 percent).{{1}} The monthly estimate for 1 October 2026 is 122.69 million, based on the 2020 census and due to be rebased on the 2025 census from the November 2026 report.{{2}}

Final figures for 2025 show 671,270 births among Japanese nationals, the lowest on record and the tenth straight annual decline, a total fertility rate of 1.14, and 1,589,533 deaths, for a natural decrease of 918,263.{{6}} Life expectancy at birth was 81.35 years for men and 87.33 years for women, and Japanese women ranked first among the countries the ministry compared.{{7}} The National Institute of Population and Social Security Research projects a population of 87 million in 2070.{{10}} For a foreign academic medical center, this points to demand centered on geriatric, oncology and chronic disease care in a shrinking, long-lived population.

government.narrative:
Japan is a parliamentary system under a constitution in which the Emperor is the symbol of the State.{{1}} The Diet, made up of the 465-member House of Representatives and the 248-member House of Councillors, is the sole law-making organ, and it designates the Prime Minister, who leads a Cabinet collectively responsible to it.{{1}}{{2}}

Sanae Takaichi of the Liberal Democratic Party became the 104th prime minister in October 2025 and was designated the 105th in February 2026, after the party won 316 of the 465 House of Representatives seats in the 8 February election.{{3}}{{4}} She reshuffled the cabinet on 17 September 2026, keeping Kenichiro Ueno as health minister and bringing in the first minister from the coalition partner, the Japan Innovation Party.{{5}}{{6}} House members serve four-year terms, so the next general election is due by early 2030 unless the House is dissolved sooner, and half of the House of Councillors next stands for election in 2028.{{1}} Health policy and the fee schedule are set nationally, and prefectures develop regional care delivery.{{7}}

economy.narrative:
Japan's economy was about 7.03 trillion international dollars at purchasing power parity in 2025, or about 57,040 per person, which the IMF ranks fifth in the world and puts at 3.3 percent of world GDP.{{1}}{{2}}{{3}} The IMF puts real growth at 1.2 percent in 2025.{{4}} The Cabinet Office's first preliminary estimate, released on 16 November 2026, showed real GDP essentially flat in July to September 2026, edging down less than 0.1 percent from the previous quarter, the first decline in four quarters, after growth of 0.4 percent in April to June.{{5}} Household consumption fell 0.3 percent, while private nonresidential investment rose 1.6 percent.{{5}} A second preliminary estimate is due on 8 December 2026.{{5}}

Monetary policy has tightened. The Bank of Japan raised its overnight call rate guideline to about 1.0 percent in June and about 1.25 percent in September 2026, and kept it at about 1.25 percent on 30 October in an 8 to 1 vote.{{6}}{{7}}{{8}} The Bank also decided to raise the pace of its exchange-traded fund sales to about ¥860 billion (US$5.48 billion) a year on a book-value basis, starting in January 2027.{{8}} Inflation and wage growth are also raising costs for hospitals, which the Health System section covers.

disease_prevalence.narrative:
The health ministry recorded 1,589,533 deaths in 2025 in its final figures, 15,845 fewer than in 2024.{{1}} Malignant neoplasms were the leading cause with 378,829 deaths (23.8 percent of the total).{{1}} Heart disease excluding hypertensive disease caused 220,539 deaths (13.9 percent), senility 214,712 (13.5 percent) and cerebrovascular disease 100,361 (6.3 percent).{{1}} Pneumonia caused 84,021 deaths and aspiration pneumonia 64,396, the fifth and sixth causes.{{1}}

WHO estimates that 17.1 percent of adults smoked in 2025, down from 33.4 percent in 2000, and that 24.4 percent of adults were overweight and 5.9 percent had obesity in 2024.{{2}}{{3}}{{4}} This suggests sustained demand in oncology, cardiology, neurology and geriatric care.

public_system.narrative:
Japan's statutory health insurance provides universal coverage, funded mainly by taxes and individual contributions, and enrollment in either an employment-based or a residence-based plan is required.{{1}} As of March 2024, the Japan Health Insurance Association plan covered 39.54 million people, society-managed plans 28.03 million, National Health Insurance 25.66 million and the system for people aged 75 and over 19.79 million.{{2}} Patients usually pay 30 percent of costs, children before compulsory schooling pay 20 percent, people aged 70 to 74 pay 20 percent (30 percent at higher incomes), and people aged 75 and over pay 10 percent (20 or 30 percent at higher incomes), with monthly out-of-pocket caps.{{2}}

The national government sets the fee schedule and prefectures develop regional delivery, and patients need no GP registration and no referral at clinics, according to a 2020 Commonwealth Fund profile.{{1}} In fiscal 2024, insurance premiums supplied 50.3 percent of national medical expenditure, public funds 37.4 percent and patient payments 11.8 percent.{{3}} Fees are revised every two years, and the latest revision raised the main portion by 3.09 percent on average over fiscal 2026 and 2027 (2.41 percent in fiscal 2026 and 3.77 percent in fiscal 2027, from June 2026), while drug prices were cut 0.86 percent from April 2026.{{4}}

private_system.narrative:
Most hospitals are run by private or other nonprofit corporations. At the end of August 2026 Japan had 7,941 hospitals with 1,440,637 beds, 105,754 general clinics and 64,940 dental clinics.{{1}} Medical corporations ran 5,550 hospitals with 816,811 beds, against 179 prefectural and 574 municipal hospitals, 140 under the National Hospital Organization and 47 national university hospitals; companies ran 23 hospitals, and individuals owned 37,950 clinics.{{1}} National, prefectural, municipal and local independent administrative bodies together ran about 1,200 hospitals, roughly 15 percent of the total.{{1}}

Hospital finances are strained. In the ministry's survey for fiscal 2024, covering 1,167 hospitals, general hospitals other than psychiatric ones had an average profit margin of minus 7.3 percent, and minus 3.9 percent after adding subsidies and other non-operating income; the margin was minus 1.0 percent at medical corporations and minus 18.5 percent at public hospitals, while clinics run by medical corporations earned plus 4.8 percent.{{2}}

financing.narrative:
Current health expenditure was 10.74 percent of GDP in 2023, down from a peak of 12.32 percent in 2022 and close to the 10.67 percent of 2012, according to WHO's Global Health Expenditure Database.{{1}} Spending per person was US$3,638 in 2023.{{2}} In 2023 the share of GDP was above South Korea's 8.57 percent and below the United Kingdom's 10.99, France's 11.52, Germany's 11.74 and the United States' 16.69 percent.{{1}} Out-of-pocket spending was 12.24 percent of current health expenditure, and domestic general government spending was 84.83 percent.{{3}}{{4}} 

The health ministry's own series puts fiscal 2024 national medical expenditure at ¥48.81 trillion (US$311 billion), or ¥394,300 (US$2,510) per person and 7.60 percent of GDP, a lower share than WHO's current health expenditure measure.{{5}} People aged 65 and over accounted for 60.1 percent of it.{{5}}

workforce.narrative:
Japan had 347,772 registered physicians at the end of 2024, or 280.9 per 100,000 people, up 1.3 percent from 2022, along with 103,652 dentists and 329,045 pharmacists.{{1}} WHO's series gives 26.49 medical doctors per 10,000 people in 2022, slightly below the ministry's 274.7 per 100,000 for the same year.{{1}}{{2}} WHO's latest values are 26.63 for South Korea (2023), 26.54 for the United States (2022), and 33.54, 40.09 and 45.93 for the United Kingdom, France and Germany (all 2023), against 23.1 for the Western Pacific Region and 34.5 for high-income countries (both 2024).{{2}} Nursing and midwifery personnel numbered 124.44 per 10,000 people in 2022.{{3}} The Finance Ministry expects supply and demand for doctors to balance around 2029 to 2032 and to tilt toward oversupply afterward.{{5}}

The ministry counted 1,440,637 hospital beds in August 2026, about 117 per 10,000 people.{{6}}{{8}} WHO's higher figure of 125.87 beds per 10,000 for 2022 is consistent with the ministry's 2022 counts of 1,492,957 hospital beds plus 80,436 general clinic beds, so the two measures should not be compared directly.{{4}}{{7}}

outlook.narrative:
Demand will keep rising as the population ages. At the 2025 census, 36.14 million people, 29.4 percent of the population, were 65 or older.{{1}} The national institute projects the share aged 65 and over rising from 28.6 percent in 2020 to 38.7 percent in 2070, while the population falls to 87 million.{{2}} In fiscal 2024, spending on people 65 and over was ¥29.35 trillion (US$187 billion), or ¥809,800 (US$5,160) per person, against ¥222,300 (US$1,420) for those under 65.{{3}}

Policy is aimed at keeping providers solvent. The government agreed to raise the main portion of fees by 3.09 percent on average over fiscal 2026 and 2027 (2.41 percent, then 3.77 percent) while cutting drug prices 0.86 percent, so the overall revision is the first net increase in 12 years and the first main-portion rise of 3 percent or more in about 30 years.{{4}}{{5}} Finances are the constraint: general hospitals averaged a profit margin of minus 7.3 percent in fiscal 2024, and public hospitals minus 18.5 percent.{{6}} On supply, the Finance Ministry expects a doctor surplus after 2032 and has proposed cutting medical school enrollment.{{7}} For a foreign partner, the openings lie in research, training and specialized clinical collaboration rather than in filling capacity gaps.

competitive_landscape.narrative: The tracker below lists 66 active partnerships with 64 foreign institutions, 19 of them US academic medical centers, mostly research ties. The National Cancer Center Japan's August 2026 list names MD Anderson, Dana-Farber, Massachusetts General Hospital and Mount Sinai.{{1}} In February 2025 Kanagawa Prefecture, Ohio State's Wexner Medical Center, Tokushukai and Japan Airport Terminal agreed to plan a clinic at Haneda Airport.{{2}}
competitive_landscape.closing: Japan is working to attract international patients. An estimated record 42,683,600 foreign visitors arrived in 2025, up 15.8 percent, but short-term visitors are excluded from public health insurance and no national database of their emergency hospitalizations exists.{{3}}{{4}} Hospitals accredited by Medical Excellence JAPAN admitted 2,099 new international patients in fiscal 2024, and the group launched a patient portal on 12 November 2026.{{5}}{{6}} No official count of medical travelers or of Japanese patients treated abroad was found.

resolution_log: World Bank Indicators API (api.worldbank.org) timed out on every request, so japan_wb.json was not available and no World Bank pages could be read. Spending, workforce and bed series use the WHO Global Health Observatory API (Global Health Expenditure Database and Health Workforce indicators), which was readable. WHO's series for doctors is lower than the ministry's registration count, so both are shown and labeled.
The OECD average could not be read (oecd.org returned 403), so the workforce chart uses WHO regional and high-income group averages for 2024 instead.

Not readable from this environment, so not cited: mofa.go.jp pages (403), Commonwealth Fund international site (403), OECD Health at a Glance (403). The Commonwealth Fund overview used is the December 2020 PDF, so structural points (coverage shares, cost-sharing, ownership in 2016) predate 2026. Kozu (2006) describes the medical education pathway; the 2023 Akatsu article confirms the national exam, matching process and 82 schools.

Fiscal 2024 national medical expenditure (published 30 October 2026) is the ministry's own definition, so its 7.60 percent of GDP differs from WHO's current health expenditure share of 10.74 percent for 2023. Yen amounts use the repository rate of 157.05 yen per US dollar (22 October 2026).

Largest private hospital group data (Tokushukai, Shinkokai, Seirei, Kameda) could not be reliably sourced to hospitals or beds, so the market chart uses WHO hospital beds per 10,000 people. The competitive landscape cites only pages read directly; other tracker leads in tracker_combined.json were not re-verified here.

The Prime Minister's reshuffle of 17 September 2026 appears in news coverage that could not be read, so it is not in the text; the Cabinet Office page confirms Takaichi as the 105th Prime Minister since 18 February 2026.

Research pass 17 November 2026; three independent verification passes, resolved by the lead editor, with every flagged point re-checked on its source page and single-verifier points checked with extra care.

Corrected: fiscal 2026 medical fee revision restated as a two-year average (3.09 percent; 2.41 percent in fiscal 2026 and 3.77 percent in fiscal 2027) per the MHLW document, drug price cut 0.86 percent (0.87 percent with materials), net 2.22 percent on the same average basis; 'largest since 1996' (Jiji, which also wrongly said 'in fiscal 2026') replaced by the Japan Times wording, a main-portion rise of 3 percent or more for the first time in about 30 years; fee changes took effect April and June 2026.

Updated: GDP to the 16 November 2026 first preliminary estimate for July to September 2026 (about flat, first fall in four quarters); 195 economies count dropped (the IMF site could not be reopened to settle 195 versus 197); Bank of Japan sentence now cites the June, September and October statements and drops the unsupported 'highest since April 1995' phrase; final 2025 vital statistics (30 September 2026) and the 2025 census (29 September 2026) replace preliminary and 2020-based figures, with the monthly estimate labeled as 2020-census-based.

Government: added the 8 February 2026 election (LDP 316 of 465 seats), the 17 September 2026 reshuffle and next election timing (four-year House of Representatives term; half of the House of Councillors in 2028, from Articles 45 and 46). The Prime Minister's Office profile lists Takaichi as the 104th prime minister (October 2025) and the 105th (February 2026), so both numbers stay, each with its date.

Health system: copayment rates and subscriber counts from the MHLW 2025 annual report (2020 Commonwealth Fund shares dropped; 2016 ownership share and the 70 percent private insurance figure replaced by August 2026 MHLW ownership counts); hospital margins now cited to the MHLW survey; medical school enrollment claims cited to the Finance Ministry paper (the 274 to 340 doctors per 100,000 projection was dropped because the primary paper does not state it); physician exam updated to 400 questions over two days, Tohoku Medical and Pharmaceutical University (2016) added before IUHW (2017), typeset.io link replaced by the Academic Medicine record; WHO bed series (125.87) reconciled with the MHLW count (about 117) in the text and in the market chart.

Added: JNTO source for 42,683,600 arrivals, Japan International Hospitals new patient counts (2,262 in fiscal 2023 and 2,099 in fiscal 2024 at 39 hospitals) from the Medical Excellence JAPAN author's article, and the direct Medical Excellence JAPAN release dated 12 November 2026. No official count of medical travelers exists. A METI study group estimate of 20,000 to 30,000, found only in a secondary article, was left out.

Recent developments kept at five health-sector items; the reshuffle and the Bank of Japan decision were not added because they are not health-sector news. Unresolved: IMF data vintage (the DataMapper pages could not be reopened), and the NCC partner list gives no signing dates for the US partners.
